solution: Pyramid B. Its base is the narrowest of the three, and the chapter describes this shape as one where the base gets narrower while the apex is broader, indicating lower percentages of younger people.

Pyramid A. Its apex is the narrowest of the three. The chapter explains that a broad base with a narrowing apex shows that more people die at each higher band, so few survive into the older age groups.

Pyramid A. A broad base means a high number of children, and the bars shorten at every higher band, so the population is concentrated in the younger age groups. The chapter calls this shape expansive and links it to a high birth rate and a high death rate.

Pyramid B. Its longest bars are in the 55 to 70 bands, so it has the largest elderly population of the three. The chapter states that a growing population in the age group of 60 plus indicates greater expenditure for medical and health facilities for the aged population.

Pyramid C. Its bars are almost equal from the base up to about age 60, so the 15 to 59 working age group makes up the largest share of the three.

The chapter supplies the reasoning. A larger size of the population in the age group of 15-59 years indicates the chances of having a larger independent working population, and a higher proportion of working population means a large number of manpower. It also warns that both extremes, old age dependency as well as young age dependency, are a severe burden on the economy. Pyramid A carries young age dependency and pyramid B carries old age dependency, so only C avoids both.

Pyramid A represents a developing country, and pyramids B and C represent developed countries.

The chapter links each shape to its birth and death rates. The expansive shape of A shows a high birth rate and a high death rate, which is characteristic of a developing country. The constrictive shape of B shows a low birth rate and lower death rates, and the stationary shape of C shows a very low birth rate and a very low death rate with a population that hardly grows. Both of those belong to developed countries.

India belongs to the expansive type. The chapter defines this as a broad base with a narrowing apex, which is exactly what fig. 2.2 shows: the bands from 0-5 to 15-20 are all close to the maximum of about 42 to 45 million for each sex, and every band above them is shorter than the one below.

India's population is a young one. The four bands from 0-5 to 15-20 are the longest in the pyramid, so children and adolescents form a very large share of the total, and the apex above 80 is very narrow, so the elderly form a small one.

The chapter draws two consequences from a shape like this. Because the number of children in the 0-15 group is high, the dependency ratio is high, which is a burden on the economy. At the same time the broad bands just below and around 15-20 are about to enter the 15-59 working age group, which indicates the chance of a large independent working population and therefore a large manpower in the years ahead.

The steady shortening of the bars at each higher band also shows that fewer people survive into the older age groups, which the chapter associates with a high birth rate and a high death rate.

The table shows India's demographic dividend across four decades. For each decade it gives the ratio of the working population to the non-working population, and the percentage of the population that is working. The last two decades, 2021-30 and 2031-40, are projections rather than recorded figures.

The two columns move together, because they measure the same thing in two ways. When the ratio of working to non-working population rises, the percentage of working population rises with it: 1.33 : 1 goes with 57.1 per cent, 1.53 : 1 with 60.5 per cent and 1.81 : 1 with 64.4 per cent. When the ratio falls back to 1.72 : 1 in 2031-40, the percentage falls with it to 63.2.

A rising ratio means more people working and fewer to support, which is what the chapter calls the demographic dividend.

The chapter explains that the ratio between working and non-working dependent population determines how productive the country is economically, and that the higher the ratio, the higher will be the contribution of the working population to the economy. With fewer people to support and more people working, the economy's resources are invested in other areas to accelerate economic development, and per capita income increases over time.

The chapter lists the forms this takes: personal savings can grow and be used to stimulate the economy; with fewer children, parents can invest more in their education, so human capital is built; more women join the labour force and contribute to economic growth; and per capita GDP increases because the dependency ratio has fallen.

It adds that these benefits are not achieved automatically. They depend on whether the government implements the right policies in areas such as education, health and research, and on the level of schooling, employment, frequency of childbearing, tax incentives, health programmes and pension and retirement policies.

A falling ratio means the dividend is shrinking. Fewer people would be working for every dependent, so the contribution of the working population to the economy would fall, and more of the country's resources would go on supporting dependents instead of being invested elsewhere. Per capita income would grow more slowly, or fall.

The table already shows the turn beginning: the ratio is projected to peak at 1.81 : 1 in 2021-30 and then fall to 1.72 : 1 in 2031-40. The chapter notes that both extremes of dependency, old age as well as young age, prove to be a severe burden on the economy of a country.

The table shows the retirement age reforms that seven countries are implementing or considering. For each country it gives the new retirement age and the year by which it is to be reached. The chapter summarises it as showing that many countries have considered or are considering an increase in the retirement age.

Developed: Germany, the United States of America, the United Kingdom, Australia and Japan.

Developing: China and India.

The table itself supports the split. The five developed countries are all raising the retirement age within the next decade, because their proportion of children and young adults is already less or decreasing. China will not change its retirement age until 2045, and India's remains at about 60 years, because in both the younger population is still large.

The chapter gives two reasons.

First, ageing populations put increasing pressure on pension funding, retirement provisions and medical facilities, so many countries have begun raising the pensionable retirement age.

Second, life expectancy is generally increasing, so people can now work up to higher ages. The chapter gives Japan as the example: life expectancy there is around 84 years, so it is considering raising the retirement age to 70 from the present 60.

Behind both lies the age structure. The proportion of children and young adults in these countries is less or decreasing, so there are fewer young workers entering to replace those who retire.

Raising the retirement age keeps people in the working population for longer, so the ratio of working to non-working population improves and the pressure on pension funding, retirement provisions and medical facilities is eased.

It also means the economy keeps the experience of older workers rather than losing it, at a time when the proportion of children and young adults is decreasing and there are fewer young workers to replace them.

The chapter's own framework explains why this matters: a higher proportion of working population means a large number of manpower, while old age dependency is a severe burden on the economy of a country.

Because China's age structure has not yet reached the point where the change is needed. The chapter states that in China the retirement age will be changed only in 2045 because it is only then that the proportion of children and young adults is going to reduce in the age structure.

Until then China still has enough younger people entering the working age group, so it does not yet face the shortage of workers and the pressure on pensions that the developed countries in the table are already facing.

The three are linked in a chain. Rising life expectancy adds people to the older age groups, which changes the age structure by raising the proportion of the elderly and lowering the proportion of children and young adults. That change puts pressure on the economy, through pension funding, retirement provisions and medical facilities, and at the same time leaves fewer young workers entering to replace those who retire.

A country's response follows from where it stands in that chain. Where life expectancy is already high and the young population is shrinking, as in Japan, Germany, the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia, the retirement age is being raised so that people keep working for longer. Where the young population is still large, as in China until 2045 and in India today, the change is not yet needed.

The chapter adds a caution for India: given that life expectancy is likely to continue rising there, the growing proportion of young and children population should also be considered before following the developed countries.
Central Asia, with a total adult literacy rate of 100 per cent. Its male and female rates are both 100 per cent as well. Europe and Northern America is next at 99 per cent.

Sub-Saharan Africa, with a total adult literacy rate of 65 per cent. The chapter states this directly: according to the graph, the lowest literacy rate is in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its female rate of 57 per cent is the lowest single figure anywhere in the graph.

In none of them. The chapter states that in any continent or sub-continent, the literacy rate of females is not more than men, except where there is full literacy as in Central Asia, and that it is the same in Europe and North America.

So the best that women achieve anywhere in this graph is equality, not advantage: 100 per cent for both sexes in Central Asia and 99 per cent for both in Europe and Northern America. In every other region the female rate is below the male rate, and the gap is widest in Southern Asia, where it is 63 per cent against 80 per cent.

The graph shows adult literacy rates in 2016 by region and by sex, against a world average of 86 per cent overall, 90 per cent for men and 83 per cent for women.

Regions divide sharply. Central Asia at 100 per cent, Europe and Northern America at 99, Eastern and South-Eastern Asia at 96 and Latin America and the Caribbean at 94 all sit above the world average. Northern Africa and Western Asia at 81, Southern Asia at 72 and Sub-Saharan Africa at 65 all sit below it. The chapter makes this comparison itself, noting that literacy rates in Europe, North America and Eastern and South-East Asian countries are higher than the global average, whereas they are lower in Northern Africa, Western Asia, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.

The second pattern is the gap between the sexes, and it runs the same way everywhere. Female literacy is never above male literacy in any region. Where overall literacy is high the two are equal, as in Central Asia and in Europe and Northern America; where overall literacy is low the gap is widest, 17 percentage points in Southern Asia and 15 in Sub-Saharan Africa and in Northern Africa and Western Asia.

The chapter also notes that differences in literacy are found within the same continent, so a continental average can hide a great deal.

Taken together the graph supports the chapter's claim that the proportion of literate population is an indicator of socio-economic development, and that it reveals the standard of living, the social status of females, the availability of educational facilities and the policies of the government.

The table shows the occupational structure of India over eleven decades, from 1901 to 2011. It gives the percentage of the working population engaged in the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors at each census, with the primary sector broken into cultivators, agricultural labourers, livestock, forestry and fishing, and mining and quarrying; the secondary into manufacturing and construction; and the tertiary into trade and commerce, transport, storage and communications, and other services. Each column totals 100 per cent.

The primary sector, in 1951, when it stood at 72.7 per cent. It is the highest single figure anywhere in the table. The primary sector is in fact the largest in every one of the eight years shown, never falling below 48.96 per cent.

The secondary sector, in 1951, when it stood at 10.0 per cent. That is the lowest sector figure anywhere in the table. The secondary sector is the smallest of the three in 1901, 1951, 1961, 1971, 1981 and 1991, and only passes the tertiary sector's 1901 level in the last two censuses.

In the secondary and the tertiary sectors, and the rise is sharpest in the last three censuses.

The secondary sector moves from 12.5 per cent in 1901 to 23.52 per cent in 2011, nearly doubling, with most of the gain after 1991. The tertiary sector moves from 15.6 per cent in 1901 to 27.52 per cent in 2011, and by 2011 it is the second largest of the three.

In the primary sector. It holds around 72 per cent from 1901 to 1971, then falls steadily: 69.4 per cent in 1981, 67.4 in 1991, 57.4 in 2001 and 48.96 in 2011. Within it the sharpest fall is among cultivators, from 50.6 per cent in 1901 to 26.4 per cent in 2011.

A multiple bar diagram is the suitable choice, because three related percentages have to be compared both within each year and across the years.

At each year draw three bars side by side, one for the primary sector, one for the secondary and one for the tertiary, using a different shading for each and giving an index. Draw every bar to the same scale.

A divided (component) bar diagram would also serve, since the three add to 100 per cent in every year; it would show each year as one bar of equal height split into three parts, which makes the changing share easier to see but the individual sector trends harder to read.

Over the eleven decades India's working population has shifted away from the primary sector towards the secondary and tertiary sectors, but the shift began late and is far from complete.

For the first seventy years almost nothing moves. The primary sector holds between 71.9 and 72.7 per cent from 1901 to 1971, and the secondary sector actually falls from 12.5 to 10.7 per cent over the same period. The change begins after 1971 and accelerates after 1991: the primary sector falls from 72.6 per cent in 1971 to 48.96 per cent in 2011, while the secondary rises from 10.7 to 23.52 and the tertiary from 16.7 to 27.52.

Within the primary sector the fall is uneven. Cultivators drop from 43.4 per cent in 1971 to 26.4 in 2011, while agricultural labourers fall much less, from 26.3 to 20.3, so a larger share of those remaining in agriculture are labourers rather than landholders.

By 2011 the tertiary sector has overtaken the secondary and the primary sector has fallen below half for the first time. The chapter's framework explains why this matters: the proportion of working population engaged in these sectors is a good indicator of the level of economic development of a nation, because only a developed economy with industries and infrastructure can accommodate more workers in the secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors, and if the economy is still agrarian then the proportion of people engaged in primary activities is high. India is moving in the direction of development, but with nearly half its workers still in the primary sector it remains a largely agrarian economy.

Besides the rural-urban division, the chapter explains population composition through:

- Age structure, the number of people in different age groups, shown through population pyramids
- Sex composition, measured as the sex ratio, the number of females per 1000 males
- Literacy and education, the proportion of literate population
- Occupational structure, the proportion of the working population engaged in the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors

The chapter's opening also names the physical and intellectual characteristics of the population as things that affect the development of a region, and it studies migration as a further influence on the structure of a population.

In every one of the six events a person or a family moves from one place to another and stays there, either for a period or permanently. The chapter's definition covers all six: when an individual or group of individuals moves from one place to another, from one political boundary to another, for a lesser or longer duration or permanently, this movement is called migration.

In each case there is also a reason for the move, and in each case the place left behind and the place moved to are both affected.

Yes, the location changes in all six events, and the reason differs in each.

Ramprasad moves from a village in Northern India to Mumbai for a job. Ritika moves from Pune to the USA for employment after her post-graduation. Sahmat and her family leave their country for a neighbouring one because of war. Babanrao moves from Marathwada to a nearby city after losses in agriculture due to drought and family problems. Ritesh moves from Pimpalwadi to Nashik for further education. Latika moves from Satara to Solapur after marriage.

The chapter notes that such movement may happen in a pre-planned manner or suddenly, and that it can be either voluntary or involuntary.

From the shortest distance to the longest:

1. Babanrao, from his village in Marathwada to a nearby city, which the event itself describes as nearby.
2. Ritesh, from Pimpalwadi to Nashik, within the same state.
3. Latika, from Satara to Solapur, within the same state but further apart.
4. Ramprasad, from a village in Northern India to Mumbai, across several states.
5. Sahmat, from her own country to the neighbouring country, crossing an international boundary but only into the country next door.
6. Ritika, from Pune to the USA, on another continent.

The first four are internal migration, because the person stays within the boundaries of the country. The last two are external migration, because the person leaves the country.

[Note: the events give no distances, so the order above is based on the descriptions the events themselves supply, that is nearby city, within the state, across states, neighbouring country and overseas.]

The reasons that appear in the six events are:

- Employment, in the offer of a job in Mumbai and in the job with a big company in the USA
- War and the need for security, which forced Sahmat's family to leave their country
- Losses in agriculture caused by drought, which forced Babanrao to sell his land
- Family problems, which the event names alongside the drought
- Education, in the move to Nashik for further study
- Marriage, in the move from Satara to Solapur

The chapter supports the split directly, stating that migration can be either voluntary or involuntary, and that it may happen in a pre-planned manner or may happen suddenly.

The willing moves are made in the hope of something better, and a person chooses the time and the destination. The reluctant moves are forced by circumstances the person did not choose, and they usually happen suddenly.

The chapter supplies several further reasons beyond the six events:

- Seasonal work. Some tribes travel seasonally in search of fodder, which the chapter calls seasonal migration, and in some places in Maharashtra more labour is needed at particular times of year.
- Better living conditions in the destination, which the chapter describes as a pull factor along with good employment opportunities.
- Higher education abroad, which the chapter gives as its own example of external migration.

The chapter supplies the effects for the rural to urban row in detail, and its account of donor and recipient regions supplies the pattern for the others: a donor region loses population, so expenditure on its facilities becomes unnecessary and its sex ratio and age structure change, while a recipient region faces pressure on its facilities but also gains a great exchange of new ideas and becomes a centre of creation, new research and new technology.

[Note: the chapter does not treat urban to rural, rural to rural or urban to urban migration separately, so those three rows apply the donor and recipient pattern the chapter does set out rather than repeating statements it makes.]

Population growth and migration are connected, because migration is one of the things that changes the population of a region.

The chapter states that migration brings changes in the population: if people migrate to a region, the population of the region will increase, and if people leave a region and migrate to another, its population will decrease.

The effect is not limited to numbers. Population density, and the patterns and structure of the population, are affected in both the original region, called the donor region, and the region migrated to, called the recipient region.

The change reaches the age and sex structure as well. The chapter's example is Kerala, where the majority of men in the working age group go to foreign countries for employment, so the state has a higher sex ratio than others, 1084 in Census 2011, and the number of children and older people exceeds the young age group. In recipient regions the sex ratio may be unfavourable instead, as in Mumbai at 832 and Pune at 948, and the working population may be higher than other age groups.

So a region's population grows or shrinks through migration as well as through births and deaths, and migration reshapes who lives there as much as how many.

A population pyramid is the graph demographers use to describe the age and genderwise distribution of a population. The Y-axis in the centre shows age groups and the X-axis shows population or percentage of population; the lengths of the bars show the numbers or percentage. The left side represents males and the right side females, the base represents the children and the apex the old people. There are three main types: expansive, with a broad base and narrowing apex; constrictive, with a narrower base and broader apex; and stationary, in which almost all age groups have the same percentage.

The sex ratio is the ratio between the number of women and men in the population, and the chapter notes that population pyramids also tell us about the number of women and men in various age groups. In India it is calculated as the total female population divided by the total male population, multiplied by 1000.

The sex ratio is important information about the status of women in a country. On average the world population reflects a sex ratio of 990 females per 1000 males. The highest has been recorded in countries like Latvia, Estonia, Russia and Ukraine, at 1162 females per 1000 males, and the lowest in Saudi Arabia at 667. Countries like China, India, Bhutan, Pakistan and Afghanistan have a lower sex ratio, and in general Asia has a low sex ratio.

The occupational structure of a population is the division of its working population, meaning women and men of the age group 15 to 59, among the various primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary occupations.

The chapter treats it as a measure of development. The proportion of working population engaged in these sectors is a good indicator of the level of economic development of a nation, because only a developed economy with industries and infrastructure can accommodate more workers in the secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors. If the economy is still agrarian, the proportion of people engaged in primary activities is high.

India's own figures show the structure changing slowly. The primary sector employed 71.9 per cent of workers in 1901 and still 72.6 per cent in 1971, but 48.96 per cent by 2011. Over the same period the secondary sector rose from 12.5 to 23.52 per cent and the tertiary from 15.6 to 27.52 per cent.

The literacy rate is the proportion of the literate population of a country, and the chapter treats it as an indicator of socio-economic development.

It reveals the standard of living, the social status of females, the availability of educational facilities and the policies of the government. The chapter adds that the level of economic development is both a cause and a consequence of the literacy rate.

Every country has its own definition of literacy. In India the literacy rate denotes the percentage of population above 7 years of age which is able to read, write and has the ability to do arithmetic calculations with understanding.

The 2016 figures show wide variation. The world adult literacy rate was 86 per cent, but Central Asia stood at 100 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa at 65 per cent. Female literacy was nowhere above male literacy: it was equal in Central Asia and in Europe and Northern America, and below it everywhere else, with the widest gap in Southern Asia at 63 per cent against 80 per cent.

Because a developed economy can absorb its workers elsewhere. The chapter states that only a developed economy with industries and infrastructure can accommodate more workers in the secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors, and that if the economy is still agrarian then the proportion of people engaged in primary activities is high.

So in a developed country most of the working population is drawn into manufacturing, construction, trade, transport and services, and only a small share is left in agriculture. The proportion of working population engaged in each sector is therefore a good indicator of the level of economic development of a nation.

India's own record shows the same relationship from the other side: as its secondary and tertiary sectors grew after 1971, the share of workers in the primary sector fell from 72.6 per cent to 48.96 per cent by 2011.

Because the literacy rate reflects several social and economic conditions at once, not just schooling.

The chapter states that the proportion of literate population of a country is an indicator of its socio-economic development, and that it reveals the standard of living, the social status of females, the availability of educational facilities and the policies of the government. A country where all four are favourable will show a high literacy rate, and one where any of them is weak will show a low one.

The relationship also runs both ways. The chapter notes that the level of economic development is both a cause and a consequence of the literacy rate: a developed economy can afford schools, and a literate population is what allows an economy to develop.

The female literacy figures show how much the indicator reveals. In 2016 female literacy was below male literacy in every region except where literacy was already near universal, and the gap was widest in Southern Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, which are the regions with the lowest overall rates.

Because the demographic dividend is measured by the ratio between the working and the non-working population.

The chapter defines demographic dividend as the growth in an economy that results from a change in the age structure of a country's population, brought about by a decline in birth rates and death rates. As fewer births are registered, the number of young dependents grows smaller relative to the working independent population.

It then states the mechanism directly: the ratio between working and non-working dependent population determines how productive the country is economically, and the higher the ratio, the higher will be the contribution of working population in the economy. With fewer people to support and more people working, the economy's resources are invested in other areas to accelerate development, and per capita income increases over time.

India's figures follow this. As the working share rose from 57.1 per cent in 2001-10 to a projected 64.4 per cent in 2021-30, the ratio of working to non-working population rose with it from 1.33 : 1 to 1.81 : 1.

The chapter adds that the benefits are not achieved automatically: they depend on the government implementing the right policies in education, health and research.

Because the chapter classifies migration by duration as well as by region, and one of those classes is temporary.

It defines migration as movement from one place to another for a lesser or longer duration or permanently, so a limited stay is migration just as much as a permanent move is.

Short-term migration can be for a limited time or seasonal. The chapter gives seasonal migration as its example: some tribes travel seasonally in search of fodder, and in some places in Maharashtra more labour is needed at particular times of year, so workers come for the season and return afterwards.

The reason for the move often decides whether it lasts. Work that exists only in one season, or study that ends with a course, brings the migrant back; employment, marriage or flight from war may not.

A population pyramid is the graph demographers use to describe the age and genderwise distribution of a population, and its importance lies in how much it shows at a glance.

It shows the structure of the population. The Y-axis in the centre gives age groups and the X-axis gives population or percentage of population, the lengths of the bars giving the numbers. The left side represents males and the right side females, so the graph carries both the age structure and the sex composition in one picture. The base represents the children and the apex the old people.

It shows the dependency burden. A larger size of population in the age group of 15-59 years indicates the chance of a larger independent working population, whereas a high number of children in the 0-15 group means a high dependency ratio, and a growing population above 60 means greater expenditure on medical and health facilities for the aged.

It allows countries to be classified. The chapter gives three main types: expansive, with a broad base and narrowing apex, showing high birth and death rates; constrictive, with a narrower base and broader apex, showing low birth rates and lower death rates; and stationary, in which almost all age groups have the same percentages, with very low birth and death rates and a population that hardly grows.

It indicates the future of a nation. The type of age structure has a direct influence on it: both extremes, old age dependency as well as young age dependency, prove to be a severe burden on the economy of a country, while a higher proportion of working population means a large number of manpower.

It is therefore the basis for the demographic dividend as well, since that depends on the ratio between working and non-working population, which the pyramid displays directly.

The rural-urban composition is the division of population on the basis of residence.

The chapter explains why the division is necessary: rural and urban life styles differ from each other in terms of their livelihood and social conditions. The age structure, sex structure, occupational structure, density of population and level of development all vary between rural and urban areas.

The general basis of the division is occupation. Rural areas are those where people are mainly engaged in primary activities, and urban areas are those where the majority of the working population is engaged in non-primary activities. The chapter notes that the criteria for differentiating rural and urban population vary from country to country, so there is no single international definition.

The two are linked by migration, and the chapter's account of recipient regions describes what happens when rural people move to urban ones: housing, water supply and transportation may prove insufficient, a large chunk of agricultural land in the peripheral regions is used for non-agricultural purposes such as housing, land prices rise, lack of housing leads to slums, public facilities are badly affected, and economic inequality and crime rates may rise. At the same time such regions see a great exchange of new ideas, become centres of creation and new research, and develop economically on a large scale.

The donor rural region is changed too: its population falls, expenditure on its facilities becomes unnecessary, and its sex ratio and age structure change, so that children and older people come to outnumber the young.

Migration changes both the size and the make-up of a country's population, and it does so in opposite directions in the two regions involved.

On numbers, the chapter is direct: if people migrate to a region, the population of the region will increase, and if people leave a region and migrate to another, its population will decrease. Population density, patterns and structure are affected in both the donor region and the recipient region.

On the sex ratio, the effect can run either way. In Kerala the majority of men in the working age group go to foreign countries for employment, so the state has a higher sex ratio than others, 1084 in Census 2011. Recipient regions may have an unfavourable sex ratio instead, as in Mumbai at 832 and Pune at 948.

On age structure, the donor region is left with children and older people exceeding the young age group, because it is the working-age population that leaves. In the recipient region the working population may be higher than other age groups.

On facilities, a donor region finds that facilities such as education and recreation are less used or not used at all, so expenditure on them becomes unnecessary. A recipient region faces the opposite pressure: housing, water supply and transportation may prove insufficient, agricultural land in the peripheral regions is taken for housing, land prices rise tremendously, lack of housing leads to an increase in slums, public facilities are badly affected, economic inequality rises and crime rates may increase.

Not all the effects on the recipient region are negative. The chapter notes a great deal of exchange of new ideas and concepts, so such regions become centres of creation and new research, development and use of new technologies is seen, and economic development takes place on a large scale.

Whether the movement is internal or external matters too. Internal migration redistributes population within a country without changing its total, whereas external migration adds to or subtracts from the national population as well.
